content: The Common Rue, scientifically known as Ruta graveolens and also referred to as Herb-of-grace, is a species of rue cultivated as an herb. It is indigenous to southern Europe. This plant is sometimes grown in gardens as an ornamental due to its bluish leaves and its ability to thrive in hot and dry soil conditions. Additionally, it is cultivated for its medicinal properties and as a condiment. In European folk medicine, rue has been traditionally used to alleviate gas pains and colic, enhance appetite and digestion, and stimulate menstruation and uterine contractions. The refined oil of rue has been historically documented as a potent abortifacient (a substance that induces abortion) by the Roman historian Pliny the Elder and the gynecologist Soranus. Rue contains pilocarpine, a compound used in veterinary medicine to induce abortion in horses, and it has been traditionally employed as an abortifacient among Hispanic communities in New Mexico. Rue can also be processed into an ointment for external application to treat conditions such as gout, arthritis, rheumatism, and neuralgia. While it has culinary applications when used sparingly, its taste is extremely bitter, and some individuals may experience significant discomfort upon ingestion. Although it was more widely used in the past, rue has fallen out of favor in modern culinary practices. Its use declined significantly during the 20th century, and it is now largely unknown to the general public and most chefs. Consequently, it is rarely available in grocery stores. Despite its decline in popularity, rue remains an important ingredient in Ethiopian cuisine, where its leaves and berries are utilized. It is also used as a traditional flavoring in Greece and other Mediterranean countries. In Istria, a recipe for grappa or rakija includes a sprig of rue. The seeds of the plant can be used in porridge, and its bitter leaves can be added to eggs, cheese, fish, or combined with damson plums and wine to create a meat sauce. Rue is also cultivated as an ornamental plant, often used as a low hedge or for its leaves, which can be incorporated into nosegays. Interestingly, most cats dislike the smell of rue, making it an effective deterrent for them.
